children.title: Position, Distance, and Displacement
children.summary: Walk to the vending machine and back and you've covered real ground, but you end up exactly where you started. Physics needs two different words for that — and mixing them up is the single most common error in this unit.
children.content:
# Position, Distance, and Displacement ## The Idea Picture walking down the hallway to the vending machine and back to your desk. Your legs did real work — you covered a solid chunk of hallway — but the moment you sit back down, you're exactly where you started. In everyday language "how far did you go" is one question. In physics it's actually two different questions with two different answers, and confusing them is one of the most common errors students make in this entire course. ## Choosing a Position Axis Before you can describe any motion precisely, you need a coordinate system. Pick an **origin** (position zero) and a **positive direction** — right, east, up, whatever suits the problem — and stick with it for the whole question. Every location along the line of motion is then a single signed number, its **position**, usually written *x* or *d*, measured in metres. ``` position (x): where an object IS, relative to the origin, with a sign ``` A position of x = −4 m isn't "negative distance." It means 4 m in whichever direction you defined as negative. The sign carries direction; the number carries magnitude. Neither one is a complete answer on its own — a position, a velocity, or a displacement without a sign (or a direction label) is an incomplete answer in this course. ## Distance: The Odometer Number **Distance** is the total length of the path travelled — every metre covered, forwards or backwards, all added together as positive numbers. It's a **scalar**: magnitude only, no direction, and it can never decrease during a trip. Think of a car's odometer — it only ever climbs, even if the car spends half the trip in reverse. ## Displacement: Where You Actually Ended Up **Displacement** is the *change in position* — a straight-line comparison of where you finished versus where you started. It's a **vector**: it has both size and direction, and in one-dimensional motion that direction shows up as a plus or minus sign. ``` Δx = x_final − x_initial ``` Displacement doesn't care what route you took, how many times you doubled back, or how long it took. Walk to the vending machine and return to your desk, and your displacement is zero — even though the distance you covered was very much not zero. ## Worked Example A cyclist starts at the 0 m mark on a straight bike path, rides forward to the 8 m mark, then rides back to the 3 m mark. Find the total distance travelled and the net displacement. **Leg 1:** 0 m → 8 m, a distance of 8 m. **Leg 2:** 8 m → 3 m, a distance of 5 m (riding backward along the path). ``` total distance = 8 m + 5 m = 13 m displacement = x_final − x_initial = 3 m − 0 m = +3 m ``` The cyclist covered 13 m of pavement but ended up only 3 m from the start, in the positive direction.
Two legs of travel (8 m out, 5 m back) add up to 13 m of distance, but the straight-line displacement is only +3 m.
## When Direction Never Reverses Real problems often involve motion that changes direction — a ball tossed up and caught on the way down, a car that overshoots a parking spot and backs up. Whenever direction reverses at some point, distance and displacement will diverge, sometimes dramatically. But if an object *never* changes direction during the interval you're studying, distance and the *magnitude* of displacement are identical — that's the one case where the distinction stops mattering numerically (though the vocabulary still matters). ## Common Mistakes - Reporting distance when a question asks for displacement, or vice versa — always check which word is used before you answer. - Dropping the sign on displacement. "5 m" and "−5 m" are different answers describing opposite directions, not the same answer written two ways. - Assuming the origin has to be where the motion starts. You can place x = 0 anywhere convenient — the physics doesn't change, only the numbers you write down. - Thinking displacement is always smaller than distance. They're only equal in magnitude when the object never reverses direction; for a round trip, displacement can be zero while distance is huge. ## Quick Gut-Check You walk 15 m east, then 15 m west, then 6 m east. What's the total distance you covered, and what's your final displacement from where you started? Work it out before moving to the next lesson.

children.title: Speed and Velocity
children.summary: Two runners finish a winding 5 km trail race in the exact same time. Same speed? Sure. Same velocity? Not even close — and in physics those two words are not interchangeable.
children.content:
# Speed and Velocity ## The Idea Two runners finish a winding 5 km trail race in the exact same time. Did they have the same speed? Reasonably, yes — they covered the same distance in the same time. Did they have the same *velocity*? That question barely makes sense for a race that loops around a park, because velocity cares about where you end up relative to where you started, not how much ground you covered getting there. ## Average Speed **Average speed** is a scalar: total distance travelled divided by the total time taken. ``` average speed = total distance / total time ``` It's always positive (or zero), it never cares about direction, and it's exactly what a car's speedometer would show you *on average* over a trip — actually, a speedometer shows instantaneous speed, which we'll get to below. ## Average Velocity **Average velocity** is a vector: the *displacement* divided by the elapsed time. ``` v_avg = Δx / Δt = (x_final − x_initial) / Δt ``` Because it's built from displacement rather than distance, average velocity can be zero (a round trip), negative (net motion in the negative direction), or wildly different in magnitude from the average speed of the same trip. In Ontario physics courses, velocity is often written with a direction tag in square brackets instead of a bare sign — for example "12 m/s [E]" or "8.0 m/s [W]" — which is just another way of carrying the same directional information the ± sign carries in a strict number-line setup. ## Worked Example A jogger runs once around a 400 m track in 100 s, finishing at the same point where she started. Find her average speed and average velocity. ``` average speed = 400 m / 100 s = 4.0 m/s ``` Since she finishes exactly where she started, displacement Δx = 0 m, so: ``` average velocity = 0 m / 100 s = 0 m/s ``` Same trip, wildly different answers — 4.0 m/s of average speed, but 0 m/s of average velocity, because "average velocity" only tracks the straight-line change in position. Now a trip that doesn't loop: a car drives 250 km due east along a straight highway in 2.5 h. Here distance and the magnitude of displacement are the same (the car never reverses), so: ``` average velocity = 250 km / 2.5 h = 100 km/h [E] ``` ## Instantaneous vs. Average Everything above describes *average* velocity — a single number that smooths out an entire interval. The number on a speedometer at any given moment is **instantaneous speed**, the speed (or velocity, if you also know the direction) *right now*, at one instant, rather than averaged over a stretch of time. A car can have wildly different instantaneous speeds throughout a trip — 0 km/h at a red light, 110 km/h on the highway — even while its average speed for the whole trip sits somewhere in between. You'll see instantaneous velocity again when we look at position-time graphs: it's the slope of the graph at a single point, versus average velocity, which is the slope between two points.
One full lap: 400 m of distance travelled, but zero net displacement since the runner returns to the starting point.
## Units and Consistency Watch your units closely — km/h and m/s show up constantly in the same course, sometimes the same problem, and they are not interchangeable without converting. To go from km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6; to go the other way, multiply by 3.6. ``` 100 km/h = 100 / 3.6 = 27.8 m/s ``` Pick one unit system per problem and convert everything into it before you start substituting numbers. ## Common Mistakes - Using total distance over total time when a question specifically asks for average *velocity* — check whether the trip involves any reversal in direction first. - Dropping direction from a velocity answer. "60 km/h" is a speed; "60 km/h [N]" is a velocity. - Assuming average velocity is simply the average of the initial and final instantaneous velocities — that shortcut only works when acceleration is uniform (more on that two lessons from now). - Mixing km/h and m/s mid-calculation without converting first. ## Quick Gut-Check A hiker walks 3.0 km north in 45 minutes, then realizes she forgot something and walks 1.0 km south back along the same trail in 15 minutes. What was her average speed for the whole trip, and what was her average velocity? Try both before checking your work.

children.title: Acceleration
children.summary: A dragster hits 100 km/h in under two seconds and you feel your body pressed into the seat. Velocity is how fast you're moving — acceleration is how fast that velocity itself is changing, and your body actually feels the second one.
children.content:
# Acceleration ## The Idea A dragster launches off the line and hits 100 km/h in under two seconds. You feel your body pressed back into the seat — but notice, that shove isn't really about how *fast* the car is going. A car cruising at a constant 100 km/h on the highway produces no such feeling at all. What you feel during the launch is how quickly the *velocity itself* is changing. That's acceleration, and it's a genuinely different quantity from velocity, not just a fancier version of it. ## Defining Acceleration **Average acceleration** is the change in velocity divided by the time it took to change. ``` a_avg = Δv / Δt = (v_final − v_initial) / Δt ``` Its units are metres per second, per second — written m/s². That unit is worth sitting with: it means "the velocity changes by this many m/s, every second." An acceleration of 4.0 m/s² means the velocity increases by 4.0 m/s during every second the acceleration is maintained. ## Sign Matters More Than You'd Guess Here's the part that trips people up: a **negative acceleration does not automatically mean "slowing down."** What determines speeding up versus slowing down is whether the acceleration has the *same* sign as the velocity or the *opposite* sign. - Acceleration same sign as velocity → **speeding up** (regardless of which direction that is). - Acceleration opposite sign to velocity → **slowing down** ("decelerating"). A car moving in the negative direction that speeds up has a *negative* acceleration — same sign as its negative velocity — even though colloquially "negative" sounds like it should mean slowing down. Always check both signs together, never one in isolation. ## Worked Example A car's velocity increases from 12 m/s [E] to 28 m/s [E] over 4.0 s, speeding up as it merges onto a highway. Find its average acceleration. ``` a_avg = (28 m/s − 12 m/s) / 4.0 s = 16 m/s / 4.0 s = 4.0 m/s² [E] ``` Positive, same direction as the velocity — consistent with the car speeding up. Now a braking scenario: the same car slows from 20 m/s [E] to 5 m/s [E] over 3.0 s. ``` a_avg = (5 m/s − 20 m/s) / 3.0 s = −15 m/s / 3.0 s = −5.0 m/s² → 5.0 m/s² [W] ``` The acceleration points opposite to the direction of motion ([W], while the car moves [E]) — exactly what you'd expect for something slowing down.
On a velocity-time graph, the slope of the line IS the acceleration — steeper means a bigger change in velocity per second.
## Average vs. Instantaneous Acceleration Just as with velocity, the formula above gives an *average* acceleration over some time interval. **Instantaneous acceleration** is the acceleration at one specific moment — how quickly velocity is changing right at that instant. For the uniformly-accelerating scenarios in this unit (a straight, unchanging slope on a v-t graph), average and instantaneous acceleration are the same constant value throughout — which is exactly what "uniform acceleration" means, and exactly why the next lesson's equations work as cleanly as they do. ## Common Mistakes - Assuming negative acceleration always means slowing down — check the sign of the *velocity* too before deciding. - Writing acceleration units as m/s instead of m/s² — a very easy typo that represents a real conceptual error if left uncorrected. - Confusing an object at its peak height (velocity momentarily zero) with an object that has zero acceleration — these are not the same thing, and you'll see this again in the free-fall lesson. - Forgetting acceleration is a vector — "5 m/s²" alone is incomplete without a direction or sign. ## Quick Gut-Check A ball is moving in the negative direction and its speed is increasing. Is its acceleration positive or negative? Reason it out from the speeding-up/slowing-down rule above before you answer.

children.title: Uniform Acceleration Equations
children.summary: When acceleration is constant, five quantities — initial velocity, final velocity, displacement, acceleration, and time — lock together into a tight set of algebraic relationships. Know any three, and you can always solve for the other two.
children.content:
# Uniform Acceleration Equations ## The Idea Constant acceleration is the "nice" case in kinematics — the one where motion follows a strict, predictable pattern instead of some arbitrary changing pattern. When acceleration is uniform, five quantities describing the motion — initial velocity, final velocity, displacement, acceleration, and time — are locked together by a small set of algebraic equations. Know any three of the five, and you can always solve for the other two. This lesson is essentially a toolkit: four equations, and a system for picking the right one. ## The Five Variables ``` v0 = initial velocity v = final velocity d = displacement a = acceleration (constant) t = time elapsed ``` Every uniform-acceleration problem is really just: "here are three of these five, find the other two." ## The Four Equations Each equation deliberately leaves out exactly one of the five variables, which is precisely what makes them useful — pick the equation that's missing the one variable you *don't* have and *don't* need. | Equation | Missing variable | Use when you don't have (and don't need)... | |---|---|---| | `v = v0 + at` | d | displacement | | `d = v0t + ½at²` | v | final velocity | | `v² = v0² + 2ad` | t | time | | `d = ½(v0 + v)t` | a | acceleration | Notice the pattern: whichever variable is missing from an equation is exactly the one you don't need to know (or solve for) in order to use it. Scan a problem, list the three values you're given plus the one you're asked to find, and the missing-variable column tells you immediately which row to use. ## Worked Example A plane starts from rest at the end of a runway and accelerates uniformly at 3.0 m/s². Find its velocity after travelling 450 m down the runway. **List what you know:** ``` v0 = 0 m/s (starts from rest) a = 3.0 m/s² d = 450 m t = unknown, not asked for either v = ? (what we want) ``` Time is neither given nor asked for — so reach for the equation missing *t*: ``` v² = v0² + 2ad v² = (0)² + 2(3.0 m/s²)(450 m) v² = 2700 m²/s² v = √2700 ≈ 52 m/s ``` The plane is travelling about 52 m/s (roughly 187 km/h) at that point down the runway. ## Choosing the Right Equation, Step by Step 1. Write down the five variables and fill in every value the problem gives you. 2. Circle the variable the question is actually asking for. 3. Whichever one of the five is neither given nor asked for — that's your "missing" variable. 4. Match that missing variable to the table above and use that equation. This system removes the guesswork. Most errors in this section come from skipping step 1 and trying to pattern-match the problem to an equation from memory instead. ## A Note on "Starts From Rest" and Other Common Phrases Certain phrases in a problem are code for specific numeric values, and missing them is a common way to get stuck: - "starts from rest" → v0 = 0 - "comes to a stop" / "comes to rest" → v = 0 - "constant velocity" → a = 0 (and then only `d = vt` really applies, a simplified case) - "at the same instant" → both objects share a value of t at that moment Translate the words into numbers *before* you touch an equation. ## A Second Worked Example: Solving for Time A car travelling at 20 m/s [E] brakes and decelerates uniformly at 4.0 m/s² until it comes to a complete stop. How long does braking take, and how far does the car travel while braking? ``` v0 = 20 m/s, v = 0 m/s (comes to rest), a = −4.0 m/s² (opposite to v0, since it's slowing) ``` **Find t first**, using the equation missing *d*: ``` v = v0 + at 0 = 20 + (−4.0)t t = 20 / 4.0 = 5.0 s ``` **Then find the stopping distance**, now that t is known — any of the remaining three equations will work, but `d = ½(v0 + v)t` is the least fussy since it needs no squaring: ``` d = ½(v0 + v)t = ½(20 + 0)(5.0) = ½(20)(5.0) = 50 m ``` The car takes 5.0 s to stop and covers 50 m while braking. Notice how the answer to the first part became a *known* value feeding into the second part — this "solve for one unknown, then reuse it" chaining shows up constantly once a problem asks for more than one quantity.
Braking from 20 m/s to a stop over 5.0 s: the triangular area under the line equals the 50 m stopping distance, matching the algebra above.
## Common Mistakes - Picking an equation that still contains a variable you don't actually know — always double check every symbol in the equation you chose has a known value except the one you're solving for. - Forgetting to take the square root (or accidentally taking it of the wrong side) when using `v² = v0² + 2ad`. - Assuming v0 = 0 when it isn't stated — only assume it when the problem explicitly says "starts from rest" or gives you an object beginning at a stop. - Sign errors on `a` when an object is decelerating — a braking or falling-then-rising object needs a consistent sign convention applied to every variable, not just some of them. ## Quick Gut-Check A cyclist decelerates from 8.0 m/s to a stop over a distance of 12 m. You're not told how much time this takes, and you're not asked for it either. Without solving anything yet — which of the four equations would you reach for, and why?

children.title: Motion Graphs
children.summary: A single squiggly line on a graph can tell you an object's entire story — when it sped up, when it stopped, which way it turned around — without a single word of description, if you know how to read slopes and areas.
children.content:
# Motion Graphs ## The Idea A single line on a graph can tell you an object's entire story — when it sped up, when it stood still, exactly when it turned around — without a single word of description, provided you know how to read it. Two skills unlock almost everything in this lesson: reading the **slope** of a line, and reading the **area** underneath one. Once those clicks, motion graphs stop being abstract and start being a genuinely faster way to solve problems than writing out equations. ## Position-Time Graphs On a position-time (*x* vs. *t*) graph, the vertical axis is position and the horizontal axis is time. The single most important fact about this graph: ``` slope of a position-time graph = velocity ``` - A steep line → fast motion. A flat, horizontal segment → the object is at rest (velocity = 0). - A line sloping upward (positive slope) → moving in the positive direction. Downward → moving in the negative direction. - A **straight** line → constant velocity. A **curved** line → changing velocity, i.e., acceleration. - The slope of the *tangent* line at one specific point gives the **instantaneous** velocity there; the slope of a straight line connecting two points (a secant) gives the **average** velocity over that interval. ## Velocity-Time Graphs On a velocity-time (*v* vs. *t*) graph, two facts do all the work: ``` slope of a velocity-time graph = acceleration area between the curve and the t-axis = displacement ``` A rising line means positive acceleration (speeding up if the line is in positive territory, slowing down if it's in negative territory and rising toward zero — recall the sign rule from the acceleration lesson). Crucially, area counts as **signed area**: region above the time axis is positive displacement, region below the axis is negative displacement, and they can partially cancel if a trip involves motion in both directions. | Graph type | Slope means | Area under curve means | |---|---|---| | position-time | velocity | (not generally meaningful) | | velocity-time | acceleration | displacement | ## Worked Example An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 10 m/s over the first 5.0 s, then travels at that constant 10 m/s for another 3.0 s. Find its total displacement using the area under its velocity-time graph. The first stretch is a triangle (velocity rises linearly from 0 to 10 m/s); the second stretch is a rectangle (velocity constant at 10 m/s). ``` triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 5.0 s × 10 m/s = 25 m rectangle area = base × height = 3.0 s × 10 m/s = 30 m total displacement = 25 m + 30 m = 55 m ```
The shaded triangle (25 m) plus the shaded rectangle (30 m) gives the total displacement of 55 m — the area under a v-t graph is displacement.
## Reading Direction Changes A position-time graph that curves back downward after rising tells you the object reversed direction — its velocity (the slope) went from positive to negative. On a velocity-time graph, that same reversal shows up as the line crossing from positive values to negative values, passing through zero at the exact instant the object is momentarily stationary before heading the other way. ## Common Mistakes - Confusing the *height* of a point on a graph with the *slope* at that point — height on a v-t graph is the velocity value; slope is the acceleration. - Forgetting that area below the time axis on a v-t graph subtracts from total displacement rather than adding to it. - Assuming a curved position-time graph means the object changed *direction*, when it might simply mean the object changed *speed* while still moving the same way — direction only reverses when the slope's sign flips. - Mixing up which axis is which after skimming a graph too quickly — always check the axis labels before reading anything off a graph. ## Quick Gut-Check Sketch, just in your head, the velocity-time graph for a ball thrown straight up and caught on the way down. What does the slope look like throughout, and where does the line cross zero?

children.title: Free Fall and Gravity
children.summary: Drop a hammer and a feather together and — on the Moon, in a vacuum — they hit the ground at the exact same instant. On Earth, air resistance hides that fact daily, but strip it away and gravity accelerates absolutely everything identically.
children.content:
# Free Fall and Gravity ## The Idea In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather at the same time on the Moon. With no air to slow the feather down, both hit the lunar surface at the exact same instant. On Earth, air resistance hides this fact every day — feathers drift, hammers drop — but strip the air away and gravity accelerates absolutely everything at the exact same rate, regardless of mass. That rate is the star of this lesson. ## Defining Free Fall **Free fall** is motion under the influence of gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Near Earth's surface, every object in free fall — dropped, thrown up, thrown sideways — experiences the same constant acceleration, called the **acceleration due to gravity**: ``` g = 9.8 m/s², directed toward the centre of Earth (i.e., downward) ``` Because it's constant, free fall is just a special case of the uniform acceleration you already worked with two lessons ago — every SUVAT equation applies directly, with a = g (or −g, depending on your sign convention). ## Sign Convention: Pick One and Commit Free-fall problems are where sign errors happen most often, because you have to choose a direction as positive *before* you start, and gravity always points the same way regardless of that choice. - **Down positive:** a = +9.8 m/s². A dropped object has v0 = 0 and everything (position, velocity) grows positive as it falls. - **Up positive:** a = −9.8 m/s². A dropped object still has v0 = 0, but velocity becomes increasingly negative as it falls, and displacement downward is negative. Either convention gives correct answers as long as you apply it consistently to every single quantity in the problem — velocity, displacement, and acceleration all need the same reference direction. ## Worked Example A stone is dropped from rest off a cliff 80 m high. Find the time it takes to hit the ground and its velocity at impact. (Using down-positive: a = +9.8 m/s².) ``` v0 = 0 m/s, d = 80 m, a = 9.8 m/s², t = ? d = v0t + ½at² 80 = (0)t + ½(9.8)t² 80 = 4.9t² t² = 16.3 t ≈ 4.0 s ``` Then find the impact velocity with `v = v0 + at`: ``` v = 0 + (9.8)(4.0) ≈ 39 m/s ``` The stone falls for about 4.0 s and strikes the ground moving at roughly 39 m/s (about 140 km/h). ## The Trickiest Case: Thrown Straight Up When an object is thrown upward and comes back down, students often assume that at the very top of its path, where velocity is momentarily zero, the acceleration must also be zero. **It isn't.** Gravity never switches off — the object is accelerating downward at 9.8 m/s² for the entire flight, including the instant its velocity happens to pass through zero at the peak. Velocity being zero and acceleration being zero are two completely different statements. A useful symmetry falls out of this: for an object thrown straight up and caught at the same height it was released, the time to rise equals the time to fall, and the speed on the way down (at any given height) equals the speed it had going up through that same height.
The velocity line has the same constant downward slope (−g) the whole time — including right through the moment velocity crosses zero at the peak.
## Common Mistakes - Believing acceleration is zero at the peak of a throw — only the velocity is momentarily zero there; g never turns off. - Mixing sign conventions mid-problem — switching between up-positive and down-positive partway through a solution is one of the most common sources of wrong answers in this topic. - Using the wrong value or forgetting units for g — it's 9.8 m/s², not 9.8 m/s or 9.8 without units. - Assuming heavier objects fall faster — in the absence of air resistance, mass doesn't affect the rate of a free fall at all. ## Quick Gut-Check A ball is thrown straight up with an initial velocity of 14.7 m/s and caught at the same height it was released. Using the symmetry described above, roughly how long is it in the air in total? (Hint: think about how long it takes to reach zero velocity going up, and what that implies about the trip down.)

children.title: Projectile Motion
children.summary: A basketball launched from half-court is doing two completely different things at once — coasting sideways at a steady pace and falling under gravity — and the trick to solving these problems is realizing those two motions never interfere with each other at all.
children.content:
# Projectile Motion ## The Idea A basketball launched from half-court is doing two completely different things simultaneously: coasting sideways at a steady pace, and falling under gravity exactly the way a dropped ball would. The remarkable — and extremely useful — fact about projectile motion is that these two motions happen completely independently of each other. The ball's horizontal glide has zero effect on how fast it falls, and its falling has zero effect on how fast it glides sideways. Once you accept that, projectile motion stops being a single hard 2D problem and becomes two easy 1D problems solved side by side. ## Splitting Motion Into Components Any projectile's velocity can be split into a horizontal component and a vertical component. If a projectile is launched at angle θ above the horizontal with initial speed v0: ``` vx0 = v0 cos(θ) (horizontal component, constant throughout the flight) vy0 = v0 sin(θ) (vertical component, changes due to gravity) ``` For a projectile launched purely horizontally — rolling off a table, thrown from a cliff, a ball hit dead level — the initial vertical velocity is simply zero: vy0 = 0, and vx0 = v0. ## The Two Independent Motions ``` Horizontal: constant velocity (a = 0), because gravity acts only vertically use d_x = vx0 · t Vertical: uniform acceleration (a = g = 9.8 m/s², downward) use the SUVAT equations from two lessons ago, with vy0 as the initial vertical velocity ``` The single thread connecting the two motions is **time** — both the horizontal and vertical motions happen over the exact same time interval, so once you solve the vertical motion for the total flight time, you can plug that same t straight into the horizontal equation. ## Worked Example A ball rolls off a table 1.2 m high with a horizontal velocity of 3.0 m/s. Find the time it takes to hit the floor, and how far from the table's edge it lands (its range). **Vertical motion first** (this is where gravity lives, and where time comes from): vy0 = 0, d = 1.2 m, a = 9.8 m/s². ``` d = vy0t + ½at² 1.2 = 0 + ½(9.8)t² t² = 0.245 t ≈ 0.50 s ``` **Horizontal motion second**, using the time just found: vx = 3.0 m/s (constant, unchanged by gravity). ``` d_x = vx · t = 3.0 m/s × 0.50 s = 1.5 m ``` The ball lands about 1.5 m from the edge of the table, roughly 0.50 s after leaving it.
The horizontal velocity component (vx) stays the same size the whole flight; the vertical component (vy) grows steadily due to gravity — together they trace the parabola.
## Range and Symmetric Trajectories For a projectile launched and landing at the same height (like a ball kicked off level ground), the horizontal distance travelled — the **range** — can be found the same way: solve the vertical motion for total flight time, then multiply by the constant horizontal velocity. For launches at an angle, remember that vy0 = v0 sin(θ) starts positive, passes through zero at the peak (exactly like the free-fall throw from the previous lesson), and becomes negative on the way down — while vx0 = v0 cos(θ) never changes at all. ## Common Mistakes - Trying to use one single equation, and one single time value, for both directions without first checking that time is genuinely the only variable shared between the two motions. - Believing horizontal velocity decreases over the flight because of gravity — gravity acts only vertically here (ignoring air resistance), so horizontal velocity is constant throughout. - Using v0 instead of the correct component (v0 cos θ or v0 sin θ) when the launch is at an angle rather than purely horizontal. - Forgetting that a purely horizontal launch has vy0 = 0, not vy0 = v0 — the entire initial speed is horizontal in that case. ## Quick Gut-Check A projectile is launched at an angle so that vx0 = 12 m/s and vy0 = 16 m/s. Without doing any calculation yet, which of those two numbers will change during the flight, and which one stays exactly the same throughout?

children.title: Relative Velocity
children.summary: Walk forward down the aisle of a moving plane and your velocity relative to the plane is not your velocity relative to the ground below. Every velocity is secretly a comparison between two things, and forgetting that is where a lot of wrong answers start.
children.content:
# Relative Velocity ## The Idea Walk forward down the aisle of a moving plane at a brisk 1.5 m/s, and your velocity relative to the plane is 1.5 m/s forward — but your velocity relative to the ground below is your walking speed *plus* the plane's cruising speed, since the plane itself is moving too. Every velocity you've calculated so far in this unit was secretly a comparison between two things: the object, and whatever it's moving relative to. Usually that second thing is "the ground," so it's easy to forget it's even part of the picture — until you meet a problem where it isn't the ground. ## The Relative Velocity Equation When an object moves through a moving medium (air, water) that is itself moving relative to the ground, its velocity relative to the ground is the **vector sum** of its velocity relative to the medium and the medium's velocity relative to the ground: ``` v_PG = v_PA + v_AG ``` Read this as: "velocity of the Plane/Person relative to the Ground equals velocity relative to the Air/current, plus velocity of the Air/current relative to the Ground." The subscripts are designed to chain together — the inner two letters (A, A) match and effectively "cancel," leaving the outer pair (P...G) on the left. Because this is vector addition, you cannot just add the magnitudes unless the two vectors point in exactly the same (or exactly opposite) direction. When they're at an angle to each other — the classic case — you need components or the Pythagorean theorem. ## The Classic River-Crossing Problem A boat aimed straight across a river doesn't actually travel straight across, relative to the shore — the current pushes it downstream the whole time it's crossing. Its resultant velocity relative to the shore is the vector sum of its own heading (relative to the water) and the current's velocity (relative to the shore). Since those two vectors are perpendicular in the simplest version of this problem, the resultant's magnitude comes from the Pythagorean theorem, and its direction from a bit of trigonometry. ## Worked Example A boat can travel at 4.0 m/s [E] relative to the water, heading straight across a river. The river itself flows at 1.5 m/s [S]. Find the boat's resultant velocity relative to the shore. The two component vectors are perpendicular (east and south), so: ``` magnitude: v = √(4.0² + 1.5²) = √(16 + 2.25) = √18.25 ≈ 4.3 m/s direction: tan(θ) = 1.5 / 4.0 = 0.375 θ = tan⁻¹(0.375) ≈ 20.6° (measured from east, toward south) ``` So the boat's actual path relative to the shore is about 4.3 m/s, angled roughly 21° south of east — noticeably drifted downstream from where it was pointed, even though its heading never changed.
The boat's heading (east) and the river's current (south) are the two legs of a right triangle; the resultant velocity relative to the shore is the diagonal.
## Aiming to Compensate for Drift A related, slightly trickier version of this problem: instead of asking where a straight-across heading ends up, you're asked how to *aim* the boat so it actually lands directly across the river, cancelling the drift. That requires angling the boat's heading partly into the current, so that one component of its water-relative velocity exactly cancels the current — leaving only forward progress across the river in the resultant. The same v_PG = v_PA + v_AG relationship still applies; you're just solving for a different unknown vector in it. ## Common Mistakes - Adding magnitudes directly (e.g., 4.0 + 1.5 = 5.5) when the two vectors aren't parallel — that shortcut only works for vectors pointing along the same line. - Mixing up which vector is being asked for — the boat's *heading* (relative to water) versus its *resultant path* (relative to shore) are genuinely different vectors, and a problem might give you one while asking for the other. - Measuring the resultant's angle from the wrong reference direction — always state clearly which axis (e.g., east) the angle is measured from. - Forgetting that "aiming upstream" to compensate for current changes the boat's water-relative heading, not the current itself — the current vector stays fixed throughout. ## Quick Gut-Check A plane has an airspeed of 200 km/h [N] relative to the air, and a wind is blowing at 40 km/h [E] relative to the ground. Without calculating the exact numbers yet, will the plane's resultant ground speed be greater than, less than, or equal to 200 km/h? And will its ground path point due north, or off to one side?

children.title: Newton's First Law
children.summary: Slam the brakes and your coffee keeps going — not because it 'wants' to spill, but because nothing was pushing it to stop. Newton's First Law is really a law about what does NOT need explaining: constant velocity.
children.content:
# Newton's First Law ## The Idea You're riding in a car that suddenly brakes hard, and your body lurches forward. Most people's instinct is to say "something pushed me forward." Nothing did. Your body was moving at the car's original speed, and when the car slowed down, you didn't — until the seatbelt (a real force) yanked you back. The car changed motion; you, briefly, didn't. That's the whole idea behind Newton's First Law: **objects don't need a reason to keep doing what they're already doing**. They only need a reason — a net force — to change what they're doing. Constant velocity (including zero velocity) is the "default" state of the universe, not something that requires upkeep. ## The Law Itself Newton's First Law, sometimes called the **Law of Inertia**, states: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity (same speed, same direction), unless acted on by a **net external force**. ``` If F_net = 0, then Δv = 0 (velocity is constant — including "constant at zero") ``` **Inertia** is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its velocity. It's not a force — it's a property of matter, and it's directly tied to **mass**. A loaded shopping cart is harder to start moving *and* harder to stop than an empty one, for the same reason: more mass means more inertia, and inertia doesn't care whether the change you're resisting is speeding up, slowing down, or turning. Notice the phrase "net external force." A book sitting on a table has forces on it — gravity pulling down, the table pushing up — but they cancel. Zero *net* force, so the book obeys the First Law and stays put. The First Law isn't about the absence of forces; it's about the absence of an *unbalanced* one. ## Why We Needed This Law At All Before Newton (and Galileo, who did much of the groundwork), the dominant idea — going back to Aristotle — was that objects naturally come to rest, and you need a continuous force to keep something moving. That seems intuitive: push a book across a table, let go, it stops. But it stops because of **friction**, a real, external force acting the whole time it's sliding. Take away friction (imagine the book on a frictionless air table) and it would slide forever at constant velocity, no push required. This reframing matters because it changes what question you should be asking. The old question was "what's keeping this moving?" The right question is "what's making it *change* — speed up, slow down, or turn?" If the answer is nothing, you don't need to explain the motion any further. It just continues. ## Worked Example: Frictionless Puck A 2.0 kg hockey puck slides across frictionless ice at 4.0 m/s. No one touches it. What is its velocity 10 seconds later, and how much force was required to keep it moving? Since the ice is frictionless, the net force on the puck is zero the entire time. ``` F_net = 0 → velocity is unchanged v(10 s) = 4.0 m/s, same direction Force required to sustain the motion = 0 N ``` The puck needs zero force to keep sliding — the "force" intuition fails here on purpose. This is the cleanest possible demonstration of the First Law: remove friction, and constant velocity requires nothing at all.
Same velocity vector at both times: zero net force means zero change in motion.
## Common Mistakes - Thinking motion "runs out" or "wears off" on its own. It doesn't — something (usually friction or air resistance) has to actively remove it. - Believing a moving object needs a constant applied force just to keep going at constant velocity. It only needs force to *change* its velocity. - Confusing "no net force" with "no forces at all." An object can have several forces on it and still be in equilibrium if they cancel. - Forgetting that "at rest" and "constant velocity" are the *same* physical situation as far as the First Law is concerned — rest is just the special case v = 0. ## Quick Gut-Check A ball is rolling across a level floor and gradually slows down. According to the First Law, that slowing is evidence of *something* — what is it, and where is it acting?

children.title: Newton's Second Law
children.summary: Push twice as hard, and something accelerates twice as fast — unless it's twice as massive, in which case it barely budges. Newton's Second Law is the equation that ties force, mass, and acceleration together, and it's the workhorse of this entire unit.
children.content:
# Newton's Second Law ## The Idea Push an empty grocery cart and it leaps forward. Push a cart loaded with 40 kg of canned goods with the same effort and it barely creeps. Same force, wildly different result, because the *mass* is different. Now push the loaded cart twice as hard — it accelerates about twice as fast. That relationship — force in, acceleration out, scaled by mass — is Newton's Second Law, and it's arguably the single most useful equation in this course. ## The Law Itself ``` F_net = m a ``` where **F_net** (net force, in newtons, N) is the *vector sum* of every force acting on the object, **m** is mass (kg), and **a** is acceleration (m/s²), always in the same direction as F_net. A **newton** is defined so the units work out cleanly: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². Rearranged, the law also tells you acceleration directly: ``` a = F_net / m ``` Two things to lock in early, because almost every mistake in this unit traces back to one of them: 1. **F_net is a sum, not a single force.** If three forces act on a box, you don't plug any one of them into F = ma. You add them as vectors first — get the resultant — *then* divide by mass. 2. **a points the same way F_net points.** If the net force is to the right, the acceleration is to the right, full stop, regardless of which direction the object happens to be moving. ## Multi-Force Problems: Sum First, Then Divide This is where Grade 11 dynamics gets noticeably more demanding than Grade 10: real objects usually have more than one force on them, and you're expected to combine them correctly — including forces that point in opposite directions, or at angles to each other. **Recipe:** 1. Identify every force acting on the object (this is exactly what a free-body diagram is for — see that lesson). 2. Choose a positive direction and assign signs, or resolve into x/y components if forces aren't collinear. 3. Add them up to get F_net. 4. Divide by mass to get acceleration. ## Worked Example: Two Forces, One Object A 5.0 kg box sits on a frictionless floor. A 30 N force pushes it to the right, and a 12 N force pushes it to the left (someone's leaning against it). Find the acceleration. ``` Take rightward as positive. F_net = 30 N − 12 N = 18 N (rightward) a = F_net / m = 18 N / 5.0 kg = 3.6 m/s², to the right ``` ## Worked Example: Finding a Missing Force A 1200 kg car accelerates forward at 2.0 m/s². Air resistance and rolling friction together push back on it with 800 N. What forward force must the engine (through the tires) be producing? ``` F_net = m a = 1200 kg × 2.0 m/s² = 2400 N (forward) F_net = F_engine − F_resistance 2400 N = F_engine − 800 N F_engine = 3200 N ``` Notice the strategy: you found F_net *first* from the known acceleration, then worked backward to solve for the one unknown force. That's a pattern you'll use constantly in this unit — F = ma isn't just for finding acceleration, it's for finding any missing piece once you know the other two.
The engine force and resistance force point opposite ways; only the difference between them accelerates the car.
## Common Mistakes - Plugging a single force into F = ma instead of the net force — always sum first. - Forgetting that mass and weight aren't the same thing (more on that in the Gravity and Weight lesson) and mixing up which one belongs in the equation. It's always mass (kg) in F = ma. - Losing track of direction: acceleration is a vector, and its sign/direction must match the net force's, not the object's current velocity. - Assuming a large force always means large acceleration without checking the mass — a huge force on a huge mass can produce a tiny acceleration. ## Quick Gut-Check Two forces of equal size act on an object in exactly opposite directions. Without doing any calculation, what is the object's acceleration — and what does that tell you about how it's moving?

children.title: Newton's Third Law
children.summary: When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you — exactly as hard. That's not a metaphor, it's a measurable, equal-sized force, and understanding whose body each force acts on is the key to not getting tangled up in this law.
children.content:
# Newton's Third Law ## The Idea Stand on a skateboard and push against a wall. You roll backward. The wall didn't move — but *you* clearly felt something push you. That something is the wall pushing back on you, with a force just as large as the one you applied to it. Newton's Third Law says this is universal: forces always come in pairs, and the two members of a pair are always equal in size and opposite in direction. ## The Law Itself ``` F(A on B) = − F(B on A) ``` For every force one object exerts on a second object, the second object exerts a force of equal magnitude, in the opposite direction, back on the first. These are often called **action-reaction pairs**, though "action" and "reaction" is a bit misleading — neither force causes the other; they exist simultaneously, as two sides of a single interaction. ## The One Rule That Fixes Almost Every Mistake Here's the detail that trips up nearly every student the first time: **the two forces in a Third Law pair act on two *different* objects.** Never the same object. When you push on the wall, the pair is: - You push on the wall (force acts *on the wall*) - The wall pushes on you (force acts *on you*) These two forces never appear together in the same free-body diagram, because a free-body diagram shows forces on *one* object only. If you're drawing the forces on you, you include "wall pushes on me" — but never "I push on wall," because that force doesn't act on you. This also explains a common paradox: if every force has an equal and opposite partner, why does anything ever accelerate? Shouldn't the forces always cancel? They don't cancel because they act on *different objects* — F = ma only cares about the forces on the object you're analyzing. When you push the wall, the wall pushes back on you; that reaction force acts on you alone, and if it's the only horizontal force on you, you accelerate away from the wall. The force you exerted on the wall doesn't get added into your equation at all — it's not a force on you. ## Identifying the Pair To find the Third Law partner of any force, swap the two objects and reverse the direction. "Earth pulls on the ball (gravity)" pairs with "ball pulls on Earth" — same magnitude, opposite direction, acting on Earth instead of the ball. That the ball noticeably accelerates toward Earth while Earth's acceleration is undetectable is entirely a mass effect (from F = ma): equal forces, wildly different masses, wildly different accelerations. | Force | Acts on | Third Law Partner | Acts on | |---|---|---|---| | Foot pushes ground backward | ground | Ground pushes foot forward | foot (you walk) | | Rocket pushes exhaust gas down | gas | Gas pushes rocket up | rocket | | Table pushes book up (normal force) | book | Book pushes table down | table | | Earth pulls ball down (gravity) | ball | Ball pulls Earth up | Earth | ## Worked Example: Walking You push backward on the ground with 150 N as you walk. By Newton's Third Law, the ground pushes forward on you with exactly 150 N. If your mass is 60 kg, what's your forward acceleration at that instant (ignore any other horizontal forces)? ``` F_net (on you) = 150 N forward a = F_net / m = 150 N / 60 kg = 2.5 m/s² ``` Notice the force that actually appears in your F = ma is the *reaction* force from the ground — the one acting on you — not the force you applied to the ground.
Two equal-and-opposite forces, but on two different objects — only the one acting on you enters your F = ma.
## Common Mistakes - Pairing two forces that act on the *same* object (like normal force and gravity on a resting book) and calling them "action-reaction." They're not — they're two unrelated forces that happen to be balanced. A true Third Law pair is never drawn on the same free-body diagram. - Thinking Third Law pairs "cancel out" and prevent motion. They can't cancel — they act on different objects, so they never appear in the same F_net sum. - Assuming the object with less mass "loses" the force battle. Both objects feel exactly the same *magnitude* of force; it's the resulting *acceleration* (via a = F/m) that differs. - Forgetting that Third Law pairs are always the *same type* of force (both contact pushes, or both gravitational pulls) — never one push paired with an unrelated pull. ## Quick Gut-Check A large truck collides head-on with a small car. Compare the force the truck exerts on the car to the force the car exerts on the truck — are they really equal? What differs between the truck and the car isn't the force, so what is it?

children.title: Gravity and Weight
children.summary: You'd weigh about a sixth as much on the Moon — but you'd have exactly the same mass. Separating 'how much stuff you're made of' from 'how hard gravity pulls on that stuff' is the whole point of this lesson.
children.content:
# Gravity and Weight ## The Idea Astronauts on the International Space Station float around looking "weightless," yet nobody thinks they've lost mass — their bodies are exactly as much matter as before. What changed isn't the amount of stuff they're made of, it's the force pulling on that stuff. Mass and weight get used interchangeably in everyday speech, but in physics they're two completely different quantities, and mixing them up is one of the most common errors in this whole course. ## Mass vs. Weight **Mass** (m) is a measure of how much matter an object contains, and how much it resists acceleration (its inertia). Mass is measured in **kilograms**, and it does not change based on location — your mass on Earth, the Moon, or in deep space is identical. **Weight** (F_g) is the force of gravity pulling on that mass. Weight is measured in **newtons**, just like any other force, and it absolutely does depend on location, because it depends on the local gravitational field strength. ``` F_g = m g ``` Here **g** is the local **gravitational field strength** (equivalently, the free-fall acceleration), about 9.8 m/s² (or equivalently 9.8 N/kg) near Earth's surface. On the Moon, g ≈ 1.6 m/s² — about a sixth of Earth's — so an object with the same mass weighs about a sixth as much there. | Quantity | Symbol | Unit | Changes with location? | |---|---|---|---| | Mass | m | kg | No | | Weight | F_g | N | Yes (depends on g) | ## Weightlessness "Weightless" doesn't mean gravity has switched off. Astronauts orbiting Earth are still well within Earth's gravitational field — gravity there is only slightly weaker than at the surface. They feel weightless because they, their spacecraft, and everything inside it are all in **free fall together**, continuously falling around the Earth rather than into it. With nothing pushing back against them (no floor, no seat) there's no normal force to give the *sensation* of weight, even though the gravitational force F_g = mg is still very much acting on them. True weightlessness (g = 0) only happens far from any massive body; orbital "weightlessness" is really *apparent* weightlessness caused by unsupported free fall. You can feel a small-scale version of this yourself: in an elevator accelerating downward, you feel momentarily lighter, because the floor doesn't need to push up on you as hard to give you that downward acceleration. Push the elevator's acceleration all the way to g (free fall) and the floor wouldn't need to push on you at all — apparent weightlessness. ## Worked Example: Weight on Two Worlds A student has a mass of 55 kg. ``` Weight on Earth: F_g = m g = 55 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 539 N Weight on Moon: F_g = m g = 55 kg × 1.6 m/s² = 88 N ``` The student's mass — 55 kg — is identical in both calculations. Only g changed, so only the weight changed. If you tried to "convert" 539 N into a mass using Earth's g, you'd correctly get 55 kg back; try that same conversion using the Moon's g on the 539 N figure and you'd get a wrong, inflated mass — which is exactly why you should never treat weight as if it were mass.
Same mass, same-sized circle — but the weight arrow (force) shrinks with the local g.
## Common Mistakes - Saying an object "weighs 55 kg." Kilograms measure mass; newtons measure weight. It's fine to say "has a mass of 55 kg" or "weighs 539 N," never both mixed together. - Assuming mass changes in orbit or free fall. It never does — mass is intrinsic to the object. - Thinking "weightless" means "gravity isn't acting." In orbit, gravity is very much acting — it's literally what keeps the spacecraft curving around the Earth instead of flying off in a straight line. - Using g = 9.8 m/s² for problems set on other planets or the Moon — g is location-specific, and problems will usually give you the right value to use. ## Quick Gut-Check A bathroom scale in an elevator reads less than your actual weight while the elevator is moving. Under what specific condition of the elevator's *acceleration* (not just its velocity) does that happen, and why?

children.title: Friction
children.summary: A parked car doesn't need a force to stay put on a hill — friction quietly supplies exactly what's needed, up to a limit. Push past that limit and the car (or the box, or your foot on ice) starts to slide, and a slightly weaker kind of friction takes over.
children.content:
# Friction ## The Idea Try to slide a heavy filing cabinet across a carpeted floor. At first, no matter how hard you push, it doesn't budge — the floor is pushing back on it just as hard as you're pushing forward. Push harder still, and suddenly it breaks free and starts sliding, and from that point on it actually feels a little *easier* to keep it moving than it was to start it moving. That everyday experience contains almost everything you need to know about friction: it resists sliding, it has a maximum, and it behaves slightly differently once motion has actually started. ## Static vs. Kinetic Friction **Friction** is a contact force that resists relative sliding between two surfaces. There are two regimes: **Static friction** (f_s) acts when the two surfaces are *not* sliding relative to each other — it's what keeps the filing cabinet still while you're pushing but before it moves. Static friction is special because it isn't a fixed value — it automatically adjusts to match whatever's needed to prevent sliding, up to a maximum value: ``` f_s ≤ μ_s N (f_s = whatever is needed to prevent sliding, up to this max) ``` **Kinetic friction** (f_k) acts once the surfaces *are* sliding, and — unlike static friction — it's essentially constant regardless of speed: ``` f_k = μ_k N ``` In both formulas, **N** is the **normal force** (the perpendicular contact force between the surfaces) and **μ** (mu) is the **coefficient of friction**, a unitless number describing how "grippy" the two specific surfaces are together. Crucially, **μ_s > μ_k** for essentially every real surface pair — it always takes more force to *start* something sliding than to *keep* it sliding, which matches the filing-cabinet experience exactly. | | Static friction | Kinetic friction | |---|---|---| | When it applies | No relative sliding | Surfaces sliding | | Formula | f_s ≤ μ_s N | f_k = μ_k N | | Value | Variable, up to a max | Constant | | Typical size | Larger (μ_s > μ_k) | Smaller | ## Why Static Friction Has a Maximum Think of static friction as a spring-like resistance at the microscopic level — the two surfaces' rough peaks interlock, and that interlocking can only supply so much resisting force before it gives way. Below the maximum (f_s,max = μ_s N), static friction exactly cancels your applied force, so nothing accelerates and the object stays put. The instant your applied force would need *more* than μ_s N to keep the object still, the interlocking fails, the object starts sliding, and you switch over to the (usually smaller) kinetic friction formula. ## Worked Example: Does It Slide? A 20 kg wooden crate sits on a wooden floor (μ_s = 0.5, μ_k = 0.35). You push horizontally with 80 N. Does it move, and if so, what's its acceleration? ``` Normal force: N = mg = 20 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 196 N Max static friction: f_s,max = μ_s N = 0.5 × 196 N = 98 N ``` Your 80 N push is less than the 98 N maximum static friction can supply, so static friction simply matches your push (f_s = 80 N) and the crate stays put — F_net = 0, a = 0. Now push with 120 N instead: ``` 120 N > 98 N max static friction → crate starts sliding Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_k N = 0.35 × 196 N = 68.6 N F_net = 120 N − 68.6 N = 51.4 N a = F_net / m = 51.4 N / 20 kg = 2.6 m/s² ``` Notice friction *dropped* the moment sliding began — from a maximum of 98 N down to a steady 68.6 N — which is exactly why the crate seems to "lurch" once it breaks free.
Once sliding, kinetic friction opposes the motion with a constant magnitude smaller than the static maximum.
## Common Mistakes - Using μ_s in a problem where the object is already sliding (should be μ_k), or vice versa — check which regime you're in first. - Assuming static friction is always at its maximum value. It's usually *less* than μ_s N — exactly enough to prevent sliding, no more. - Forgetting that friction depends on the **normal force**, not directly on weight — on an incline or with an extra vertical force involved, N ≠ mg, and using mg instead of the actual N is a very common error (see the Free-Body Diagrams and Applications lessons). - Thinking a larger surface area means more friction. For the simple models used here, friction depends on N and μ, not on contact area. ## Quick Gut-Check Two identical boxes sit on the same floor, but one has twice the mass of the other. Does the heavier box have a higher coefficient of friction, a higher maximum static friction force, or both — and why?

children.title: Free-Body Diagrams
children.summary: Before you can solve almost any dynamics problem, you need to isolate one object and draw every single force acting on it — no more, no less. A free-body diagram is the single habit that separates students who consistently get these problems right from students who guess.
children.content:
# Free-Body Diagrams ## The Idea Ask a room of students to solve a problem about a box on a ramp without ever drawing a diagram, and you'll get a room full of different, mostly wrong answers — someone forgets friction, someone uses the box's weight where they should have used the normal force, someone points an arrow the wrong way. A **free-body diagram** (FBD) is the fix: isolate one single object, draw *every* force acting on *it alone*, and nothing else. It sounds almost too simple to matter, but it's the single most reliable habit for avoiding errors in this entire unit. ## What Goes In (and What Doesn't) A free-body diagram shows: - The object of interest, drawn as a simple dot or box. - An arrow for every force acting **on** that object, pointing in the direction the force acts, roughly scaled to size, and labeled. A free-body diagram does **not** show: - Forces the object exerts *on other things* (those belong on a different object's diagram — see Newton's Third Law). - Velocity or acceleration arrows (those describe motion, not force — don't mix them onto the same diagram, though it's fine to note acceleration's direction off to the side). - The surfaces, ropes, or other objects themselves, beyond what's needed to see where forces are applied. ## The Systematic Method 1. **Isolate.** Sketch just the object as a simple shape, ignoring everything around it except as anchor points. 2. **Gravity, always.** Every object with mass has a weight force, F_g = mg, straight down. It's the one force that's basically never absent. 3. **Contact forces.** Wherever the object touches something else, there's a **normal force** perpendicular to that surface, pushing away from it. If there's relative sliding or a tendency to slide, add a **friction force** parallel to the surface, opposing the sliding (or the tendency toward it). 4. **Applied and tension forces.** Any push, pull, or rope/string tension gets its own arrow, in the direction it's actually applied. 5. **Check your count.** No Third-Law-pair force from another object's diagram. No velocity arrows. No forces "the object exerts" — only forces exerted *on* it. ## Case 1: Hanging From a Rope A lamp of mass m hangs motionless from a single vertical rope. Only two forces act on it: gravity (F_g = mg, down) and rope tension (F_T, up). Since the lamp isn't accelerating, these must be equal in size — F_T = mg — even without knowing anything else about the rope.
Two forces only — tension and gravity — equal and opposite because the lamp hangs in equilibrium.
## Case 2: A Box on an Incline This is the classic Grade 11 diagram, and it's worth mastering because it comes back constantly in the Applications lesson. A box rests on a ramp tilted at angle θ, with friction present. Four forces act on it: gravity (straight down, always), the normal force (perpendicular to the ramp surface, *not* straight up), friction (along the ramp surface, opposing sliding or potential sliding), and possibly an applied force. The key extra step for an incline: gravity is the only force that *doesn't* naturally line up with the ramp, so it gets split into two **components** — one parallel to the ramp surface (mg sin θ, pulling the box down the slope) and one perpendicular to it (mg cos θ, pressing the box into the ramp, balanced by the normal force). ``` Parallel to ramp: mg sin θ (pulls down-slope) Perpendicular to ramp: mg cos θ (balanced by N) ```
Normal force is perpendicular to the ramp (not vertical); gravity stays vertical but gets resolved into components along and into the ramp.
## Common Mistakes - Drawing the normal force straight up instead of perpendicular to the actual contact surface — on an incline, "up" and "perpendicular to the ramp" are different directions. - Leaving gravity un-split on an incline problem, then plugging mg directly into an equation that needed only its parallel or perpendicular component. - Adding a force the object exerts on something else (violates the Third Law separation — see that lesson). - Drawing friction in the wrong direction. Friction opposes *relative sliding or the tendency toward it* — figure out which way the object would slide without friction, then draw the friction arrow opposite to that. ## Quick Gut-Check A crate sits on a truck bed while the truck accelerates forward. Sketch the free-body diagram for the crate alone (not the truck) — how many forces does it need, and which one is responsible for the crate accelerating forward along with the truck?

children.title: Applications of Newton's Laws
children.summary: An elevator floor pushes up on you a little harder when it's speeding up on the way down than when it's cruising at constant speed — your bathroom scale would actually catch the difference. Multi-force, multi-object problems are where all the individual pieces of this unit finally come together.
children.content:
# Applications of Newton's Laws ## The Idea Everything so far in this unit — F = ma, friction, free-body diagrams, gravity — has mostly been practiced one force or one object at a time. Real problems rarely cooperate like that. A box sliding down a ramp fights both gravity and friction at once. An elevator passenger feels different things depending on whether the elevator is speeding up, slowing down, or cruising. Two connected blocks share a common acceleration because a rope forces them to move together. This lesson is about combining everything you've already learned to handle those messier, more realistic situations. ## Inclines With Friction Take the incline free-body diagram from the previous lesson and actually solve it. The net force along the ramp surface is gravity's parallel component minus friction (assuming the box slides down): ``` Along the ramp: F_net = mg sin θ − f_k Perpendicular: N = mg cos θ (no acceleration perpendicular to the ramp) Friction: f_k = μ_k N = μ_k mg cos θ ``` **Worked example:** A 10 kg crate slides down a 25° ramp with μ_k = 0.20. Find its acceleration. ``` N = mg cos θ = 10 × 9.8 × cos 25° = 88.8 N f_k = μ_k N = 0.20 × 88.8 = 17.8 N mg sin θ = 10 × 9.8 × sin 25° = 41.4 N F_net (along ramp) = 41.4 N − 17.8 N = 23.6 N a = F_net / m = 23.6 / 10 = 2.36 m/s², directed down the slope ``` ## Elevators: Apparent Weight Stand on a scale inside an elevator. The scale doesn't measure your true weight (mg) directly — it measures the **normal force** the floor exerts on you, which only equals mg when the elevator isn't accelerating. Apply Newton's Second Law to you, taking up as positive: ``` F_net = N − mg = m a N = mg + m a = m(g + a) ``` Here **a** is the elevator's acceleration, positive if accelerating upward, negative if accelerating downward. - Accelerating **upward** (starting to rise, or slowing down while descending): a > 0, so N > mg — you feel heavier. - Accelerating **downward** (starting to descend, or slowing down while rising): a < 0, so N < mg — you feel lighter. - Constant velocity (or at rest): a = 0, so N = mg — the scale reads your true weight, exactly like standing on solid ground. **Worked example:** A 70 kg person rides an elevator that accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s². What does the scale read? ``` N = m(g + a) = 70 × (9.8 + 1.5) = 70 × 11.3 = 791 N ``` Compare to their true weight at rest, 70 × 9.8 = 686 N — the scale reads 105 N more while accelerating upward.
When accelerating upward, the normal (apparent weight) force must exceed gravity to also produce the upward acceleration.
## Connected Objects: Blocks and Pulleys When two objects are linked by a rope or string (assumed massless and inextensible), they share the **same magnitude of acceleration** — the rope forces them to speed up and slow down together — and the rope's tension is the same throughout an ideal, massless, frictionless-pulley string. **Worked example:** Two blocks, m₁ = 4.0 kg and m₂ = 6.0 kg, are connected by a string over a frictionless pulley at the edge of a table (m₁ on the table, frictionless surface; m₂ hangs off the side). Find the acceleration of the system and the tension. Treat the whole system's net driving force as m₂'s weight (the only thing not balanced by a normal force), divided by the *total* mass being accelerated: ``` a = (m₂ g) / (m₁ + m₂) = (6.0 × 9.8) / (10.0) = 5.88 m/s² ``` Then find tension from either block alone — using m₁ (horizontal, frictionless table, only tension acts horizontally on it): ``` F_net on m₁ = T = m₁ a = 4.0 × 5.88 = 23.5 N ``` Check using m₂ (vertical: weight down, tension up, net force causes its downward acceleration): ``` m₂ g − T = m₂ a 6.0 × 9.8 − T = 6.0 × 5.88 58.8 − T = 35.3 → T = 23.5 N ✓ ``` Both blocks give the same tension, which is a good way to check your work on any connected-object problem. ## Common Mistakes - Using mg instead of the actual normal force N when computing friction on a ramp — N = mg cos θ on an incline, not mg. - Forgetting that "elevator moving downward" and "elevator accelerating downward" are different things — apparent weight depends only on acceleration, not on velocity or direction of travel. - Assuming connected objects can have different accelerations. As long as the connecting string/rope is inextensible, their acceleration magnitudes must match. - Skipping the free-body diagram on multi-force problems and trying to combine everything in your head — this is exactly where that habit pays off most. ## Quick Gut-Check In the two-block pulley example, what would happen to the acceleration if the table surface weren't frictionless — would it increase, decrease, or could you not tell without knowing μ? Sketch how you'd modify the equations.

children.title: Uniform Circular Motion
children.summary: Swing a ball on a string in a circle and the string pulls it inward, toward your hand — not forward, not outward. That inward pull is what keeps something turning instead of flying off in a straight line, and it's not some mysterious new force of its own.
children.content:
# Uniform Circular Motion ## The Idea Swing a ball on a string in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The ball's speed never changes, yet by Newton's First Law, something must be causing it to constantly change *direction* — otherwise it would fly off in a straight line. That something is the string tension, pulling the ball inward, toward the center of the circle, at every single instant. That inward pull, and the inward acceleration it produces, is what this lesson is about — and it applies to everything from cars rounding a curve to the Moon orbiting the Earth. ## Centripetal Acceleration Even though the *speed* is constant in uniform circular motion, the *velocity* is not — velocity is a vector, and its direction is constantly changing as the object goes around the circle. A changing velocity means there's an acceleration, called **centripetal acceleration** (from Latin for "center-seeking"), and it always points from the object straight toward the center of the circle. ``` a_c = v² / r ``` where **v** is the object's speed (constant, in uniform circular motion) and **r** is the radius of the circular path. Note that a_c points toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity at every instant — velocity is tangent to the circle, acceleration points inward. ## Centripetal Force Is Not a New Force This is the single most important idea in this lesson: **"centripetal force" is not a new, separate kind of force that you add to a free-body diagram.** It's a *label* for whichever real, physical force (or combination of forces) happens to be supplying the inward pull in a given situation. By Newton's Second Law, that force must equal: ``` F_c = m a_c = m v² / r ``` - Ball on a string: the **string tension** is the centripetal force. - Car rounding a flat curve: **friction** between tires and road is the centripetal force. - Satellite orbiting Earth: **gravity** is the centripetal force. - Car on a banked curve: a **component of the normal force** contributes to the centripetal force. In every case, you find the centripetal force the same way you find any other force in a free-body diagram — you don't draw a separate arrow labeled "centripetal force" pointing inward *in addition to* tension or friction or gravity. Instead, you identify which already-existing force (or combination) is doing that job, and set its net inward component equal to m v² / r.
Velocity is always tangent to the circle; the net force (whatever supplies it) always points toward the center, perpendicular to velocity.
## Worked Example: Car on a Flat Curve A 1000 kg car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius 50 m at a constant 15 m/s. What minimum coefficient of static friction between tires and road is required for the car not to skid? Here friction is the only horizontal force available, so it must supply the entire centripetal force: ``` F_c = m v² / r = 1000 × 15² / 50 = 1000 × 225 / 50 = 4500 N Maximum available friction: f_s,max = μ_s N = μ_s (mg) [flat road, N = mg] Need: μ_s (mg) ≥ F_c μ_s ≥ F_c / (mg) = 4500 / (1000 × 9.8) = 0.459 ``` So the road/tire coefficient of static friction needs to be at least about 0.46 — below that, the car skids outward off its circular path (not because an outward "centrifugal force" flings it out, but because friction simply can't supply enough inward force to keep it turning, so it continues in a straighter line than the curve). ## Worked Example: Centripetal Acceleration Alone A satellite moves at 7.8 km/s (7800 m/s) in a circular orbit of radius 6.6 × 10⁶ m. Find its centripetal acceleration. ``` a_c = v² / r = (7800)² / (6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.08 × 10⁷ / 6.6 × 10⁶ ≈ 9.2 m/s² ``` That's close to g at Earth's surface — consistent with gravity being the sole force providing this satellite's centripetal acceleration. ## Common Mistakes - Drawing a separate "centripetal force" arrow on a free-body diagram in addition to tension, friction, or gravity — centripetal force is a role, not an extra force to add. - Invoking a mythical outward "centrifugal force" to explain why objects seem flung outward. What's actually happening is the object's inertia (First Law) carrying it in a straight line while the inward force bends its path into a circle — the "outward" sensation is your own inertia, not a real outward force acting on you. - Forgetting that in uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity (and therefore there's still an acceleration) is not — a_c exists even though the object isn't "speeding up" in the everyday sense. - Mixing up r as the diameter instead of the radius in a_c = v²/r. ## Quick Gut-Check A ball on a string is swung in a *vertical* circle rather than a horizontal one. At the very top of the loop, which direction does the string tension point, and does gravity help or hinder providing the needed centripetal force at that point?

children.title: Work and the Work-Energy Theorem
children.summary: Push a stalled car and nothing happens — physically, you've done zero work. Get it rolling and the story changes: force applied over a distance is exactly what changes an object's energy, and that link is the key to everything else in this unit.
children.content:
# Work and the Work-Energy Theorem ## The Idea Push a stalled car and it doesn't budge — you're straining, sweating, applying force the whole time, but in physics terms you've done zero work, because nothing moved. Now get it rolling and push it twenty metres down the road: *that's* work. Physics has a stingy, precise definition of the word, and it's the doorway into everything else in this unit — kinetic energy, potential energy, power, all of it trace back to this one idea: force applied over a distance changes how much energy something has. ## Defining Work **Work** (W) is done on an object when a force causes a displacement. It's not enough to push — the object has to actually move, and only the part of the force that lines up with the motion counts. ``` W = F d cos(θ) ``` - **F** is the applied force (N) - **d** is the displacement (m) - **θ** is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector - Work is measured in **joules (J)**, where 1 J = 1 N·m If you carry a backpack at constant height across a flat hallway, your arms exert an upward force but you're moving horizontally — θ = 90°, cos(90°) = 0, so technically you've done zero work on the backpack (your muscles disagree, but that's a biology problem, not a physics one). If the force and displacement point the same way, θ = 0° and W = Fd, the simplest case. If you're dragging a sled and the rope is angled up from the ground, only the horizontal component of your pull does work moving it forward. Work can also be **negative** — if a force acts opposite to the direction of motion (like friction slowing a sliding box, or air resistance on a falling leaf), θ = 180°, cos(180°) = −1, and that force removes energy from the object. ## The Work-Energy Theorem Here's the payoff: the **net work** done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. ``` W_net = ΔKE = KE_f − KE_i ``` This is huge, because it means you don't need to track an object's motion moment-by-moment with kinematics equations to figure out its final speed — you just need to know the total work done on it. It's a shortcut that becomes essential once forces aren't constant (like a spring) or the path is curvy (like a rollercoaster), situations where kinematics equations alone get messy fast. ## Worked Example A 60 kg crate starts at rest on a frictionless floor. A worker pushes it with a constant horizontal force of 150 N over a distance of 4.0 m. Find its final speed. **Step 1 — find the net work done:** ``` W_net = F d cos(θ) = (150 N)(4.0 m)(cos 0°) = 600 J ``` **Step 2 — apply the work-energy theorem:** ``` W_net = ΔKE = KE_f − KE_i 600 J = ½mv_f² − 0 (starts at rest, so KE_i = 0) 600 = ½(60)v_f² 600 = 30 v_f² v_f² = 20 v_f = 4.5 m/s ``` The crate ends up moving at about **4.5 m/s** — and notice we never had to touch acceleration or use a kinematics equation directly.
Only the force component along the direction of displacement does work: W = Fd cos(θ).
## Common Mistakes - Forgetting the angle: applying W = Fd even when the force isn't parallel to the motion. If a force is perpendicular to displacement (like gravity on something moving horizontally), it does **zero** work, no matter how strong it is. - Mixing up positive and negative work — a braking force doesn't do "negative distance," it does negative work because it points opposite to the motion. - Treating the work-energy theorem as only about *applied* forces — it applies to the **net** force, so friction, gravity, and normal force all have to be accounted for if they're doing work too. ## Quick Gut-Check A weightlifter holds a loaded barbell perfectly still above their head for ten seconds. How much work is being done on the barbell during that time, and does that match how tired their arms feel?

children.title: Kinetic Energy
children.summary: A cyclist at 10 km/h and a car at 100 km/h are both just 'moving' — but you know instinctively the car carries far more energy. Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, which is why doubling your driving speed quadruples the danger, not doubles it.
children.content:
# Kinetic Energy ## The Idea A cyclist coasting at 10 km/h and a car cruising at 100 km/h are both just "moving," but you know instinctively they're not equally dangerous in a collision — the car carries vastly more energy of motion. That's **kinetic energy**, and the reason it doesn't just scale with speed but with speed *squared* is the whole story of why doubling your driving speed doesn't just double your stopping distance — it quadruples it. ## Defining Kinetic Energy **Kinetic energy** (KE) is the energy an object has because it's moving. It depends on both mass and velocity: ``` KE = ½ m v² ``` - **m** is mass (kg) - **v** is speed (m/s) - KE is measured in **joules (J)**, same unit as work — which is not a coincidence, since kinetic energy is literally the accumulated result of work done on an object (that's the work-energy theorem from the last lesson). Two things jump out of this formula. First, KE depends on mass linearly — double the mass, double the kinetic energy. Second, and more dramatically, KE depends on velocity *squared* — double the speed and you quadruple the kinetic energy, triple the speed and you increase it ninefold. That squared relationship is why highway collisions are so much more destructive than parking-lot fender-benders, and why speed limits matter more than gut feeling suggests. Kinetic energy is a **scalar** — it has no direction.
