Over a 30-day month, that's roughly 7.5 × 30 = 225 kWh, or about $29 — a useful reality check on why space heaters show up clearly on winter power bills.

## Comparing Typical Household Loads

| Appliance | Typical power | Running 1 hour costs (at $0.13/kWh) |
|---|---|---|
| LED bulb | 10 W | ~$0.0013 |
| Laptop charger | 60 W | ~$0.008 |
| Refrigerator | 150 W | ~$0.02 |
| Microwave | 1000 W | ~$0.13 |
| Space heater | 1500 W | ~$0.20 |
| Electric dryer | 3000 W | ~$0.39 |

The table makes the physics visible: power ratings (in watts) span nearly three orders of magnitude across common devices, and since cost scales directly with both power *and* time, a high-power appliance run briefly can still cost less than a low-power one left running all day.

## Where Does the Energy Actually Go?

In a resistor, all the electrical energy delivered converts to heat — this is exactly what happens inside a toaster, kettle, or incandescent bulb filament, and it's called **resistive** or **Joule heating**. This is also why P = I²R matters practically: it's the formula engineers use to calculate how much a wire will heat up under a given current, which is exactly what determines the safe current rating of household wiring and fuses. Too much current through too little wire, and P = I²R tells you there's a fire risk — the resistance of the wire times the square of an excessive current can generate a lot of unwanted heat very quickly.

## Why Efficiency Ratings Matter

Not every device is trying to produce heat. A light bulb is meant to produce *light*, and any power that ends up as waste heat instead is, in a real sense, wasted energy. This is exactly why old incandescent bulbs (which glow because a thin filament resists current so much it gets white-hot — pure Joule heating) have largely been phased out in favour of LED bulbs. An incandescent bulb converts roughly 5% of its input power into visible light and dumps the rest as heat; an LED bulb producing the same brightness might draw only one-eighth the power, because it produces light through a much more direct process that wastes far less energy as heat. Since cost is P × t × (price per kWh), cutting the power draw for the same output directly cuts the running cost — which is exactly the comparison utility companies lean on in "switch to LED and save" campaigns.

## Common Mistakes

- Forgetting to convert watts to kilowatts (divide by 1000) before multiplying by hours to get kWh — mixing units here is the single most common error on cost calculations.
- Using P = I²R or P = V²/R with the wrong resistance — these formulas need the resistance of the *specific component* being powered, not some other resistor in the circuit.
- Treating "power" and "energy" as interchangeable — power is a rate (W), energy is a total amount (J or kWh); an appliance's wattage alone can't tell you a cost without also knowing how long it ran.
- Assuming doubling the current only doubles the power — because of the I² term, doubling current actually quadruples the power dissipated as heat.

## Quick Gut-Check

Two appliances have the same power rating, but one runs for twice as long as the other today. Without doing any calculation, which one used more energy, and how much more?

children.title: Magnetism and Magnetic Fields
children.summary: A compass needle swings to point north no matter where you stand on Earth's surface — which means the whole planet is quietly acting like one enormous bar magnet, and understanding why starts with the same field-line picture that describes a fridge magnet.
children.content:
# Magnetism and Magnetic Fields ## The Idea Hold two bar magnets close together and you can feel it before you see it — turn them one way and they snap together, flip one around and they push apart, with nothing visibly touching. That invisible push and pull is a **magnetic field**, a region of space around a magnet where magnetic forces act. This lesson covers what causes it, how we draw it, and why it's not just a curiosity — it's the same field that keeps a compass pointed north anywhere on the planet. ## Magnetic Poles Every magnet has two ends, called **poles** — a **north pole** and a **south pole** — and the fundamental rule of magnetism mirrors electric charge: - **Like poles repel**: north repels north, south repels south. - **Opposite poles attract**: north attracts south. Unlike electric charge, though, magnetic poles always come in pairs. Cut a bar magnet in half, and you don't get an isolated north pole and an isolated south pole — you get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole. No one has ever isolated a single magnetic **monopole**, despite plenty of searching; magnetism seems to fundamentally require both poles together. ## Magnetic Field Lines We visualize a magnetic field using **field lines** — imaginary lines that show the direction a compass needle would point at each location, and whose density shows the field's strength. For a bar magnet, field lines emerge from the north pole, curve around through the space outside the magnet, and re-enter at the south pole; inside the magnet itself, the lines continue from south back to north, forming closed loops. A few rules make field-line diagrams consistent: - Field lines never cross. - Lines are denser (closer together) where the field is stronger — typically near the poles. - The direction of the field at any point is tangent to the field line there.
Field lines always leave the north pole and loop back into the south pole outside the magnet, then continue through the magnet's interior from south to north — forming closed loops with no beginning or end.
## What Actually Causes Magnetism At the atomic level, magnetism comes from moving electric charge — specifically, electrons spinning and orbiting within atoms behave like tiny current loops, each producing a tiny magnetic field. In most materials these countless tiny fields point in random directions and cancel out. In **ferromagnetic materials** — iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys — groups of neighbouring atoms can lock their fields into alignment within regions called **magnetic domains**. In an unmagnetized piece of iron, domains point every which way and cancel overall; in a magnetized permanent magnet, most domains have been coaxed into pointing the same direction, so their fields add up into one strong, coherent field. ## Earth as a Giant Magnet A compass needle is just a small, freely pivoting bar magnet, and it consistently points north because Earth itself generates a magnetic field, believed to arise from the churning of molten iron in its outer core (a process called the geodynamo). Confusingly, the geographic "North Pole" is actually close to the *south* magnetic pole of Earth's internal field — that's precisely why a compass's north-seeking pole points toward it: opposite poles attract. Earth's magnetic field extends far into space as the **magnetosphere**, which deflects much of the charged particle stream from the Sun (the solar wind) and is part of what makes sustained life on the surface possible. ## Common Mistakes - Thinking you can isolate a single magnetic pole by cutting a magnet in half — you always get two new, smaller magnets, each with both a north and a south pole. - Confusing electric field lines (which start and end on isolated charges) with magnetic field lines (which always form closed loops, since there's no magnetic monopole to start or end on). - Assuming all metals are magnetic — only ferromagnetic metals (iron, nickel, cobalt, and specific alloys) respond strongly; aluminum, copper, and gold are essentially non-magnetic. - Mixing up Earth's geographic and magnetic poles — the compass's "north" pole points toward Earth's geographic north because that's where Earth's magnetic *south* pole actually is. ## Quick Gut-Check If you heat a magnetized iron nail until it glows red-hot, it loses its magnetism. Using the idea of magnetic domains, explain why heating would scramble a material's magnetic alignment.

children.title: Electromagnetism
children.summary: Coil a wire around an iron nail, run current through it, and you've just built an electromagnet strong enough to lift paperclips — proof that electricity and magnetism aren't two separate topics, they're two faces of the same phenomenon.
children.content:
# Electromagnetism ## The Idea In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed something strange during a lecture demonstration: whenever current flowed through a nearby wire, a compass needle on the table twitched and swung to align itself perpendicular to the wire. That accidental observation cracked open one of physics' biggest unifications — electricity and magnetism aren't separate forces, they're deeply linked. Moving charge creates a magnetic field, and (as you'll see) a changing magnetic field can push charge to move. That two-way link is the entire basis of electromagnets, electric motors, and generators — essentially every electric machine that spins or lifts something. ## A Current-Carrying Wire Makes a Magnetic Field Any wire carrying current is surrounded by a magnetic field, with field lines forming **concentric circles** around the wire. The strength of the field increases with current and decreases with distance from the wire. To find the *direction* of these circular field lines, use the **right-hand rule**: point your right thumb in the direction of conventional current flow, and your curled fingers show the direction the magnetic field circles around the wire.
Current flows upward through the wire. The concentric ellipses represent circular magnetic field lines (viewed at an angle) wrapping around the wire, with direction set by the right-hand rule.
## From a Straight Wire to an Electromagnet A single straight wire produces a fairly weak field. Coil the wire into a loop, and the circular fields from every turn add together inside the loop, producing a much stronger, more concentrated field. Coil the wire many times into a tight helix — a **solenoid** — and the fields combine even further, producing a field inside the coil that closely resembles a bar magnet's: strong, uniform, with a clear north and south end. A second right-hand rule applies here: curl your right-hand fingers in the direction current flows around the loops, and your thumb points toward the solenoid's north pole. Wrapping that coil around a ferromagnetic core (commonly a soft iron rod) makes an **electromagnet** — the iron's own domains align with the coil's field and dramatically boost its strength, sometimes by a factor of a thousand or more compared to an air core. Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched on and off (just interrupt the current) and its strength can be tuned by changing the current or the number of coil turns. This tunability is exactly why electromagnets, not permanent magnets, run industrial cranes that lift and drop scrap steel, MRI machines, and the solenoids inside doorbells and relays. ## Force on a Current-Carrying Wire in a Field The link runs both ways: just as current creates a magnetic field, a current-carrying wire placed *inside* an external magnetic field experiences a **force** — this is the basis of the electric motor. When current flows through a wire sitting in a magnetic field (and the current isn't parallel to the field), the wire feels a push perpendicular to both the current direction and the field direction. Reverse either the current or the field, and the force reverses too. In a real motor, a current-carrying coil sits inside a fixed magnetic field; the resulting force on each side of the coil creates a **torque** that spins the coil continuously (with a commutator flipping the current direction each half-turn to keep the rotation going the same way). ## Generators: Running the Idea Backward If a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force, the reverse relationship also holds: moving a wire *through* a magnetic field (or changing the field through a loop) induces a current in the wire — a phenomenon called **electromagnetic induction**. This is exactly how a **generator** works: mechanical energy (from falling water, wind, steam turbines, or a hand crank) spins a coil of wire within a magnetic field, and that motion induces a current that flows out to power the grid. Motors turn electrical energy into motion; generators turn motion into electrical energy — the same basic physics, running in opposite directions. ## Common Mistakes - Forgetting the right-hand rule uses *conventional* current direction (positive-charge-flow direction), not the actual direction electrons move. - Assuming a stationary charge or a wire with no current produces a magnetic field — a magnetic field from electric charge specifically requires that charge to be *moving*. - Mixing up the two right-hand rules — one for the field around a straight wire (fingers curl to show field direction, thumb along current) and one for a solenoid's overall polarity (fingers curl along the loop's current, thumb shows north pole). - Thinking an electromagnet is "just like" a permanent magnet — it needs continuous current to stay magnetized, and its strength and polarity can be changed on demand, which a permanent magnet's can't. ## Quick Gut-Check A doorbell electromagnet needs to switch on and off rapidly and needs to be strong for its size. Using what you know about solenoids, iron cores, and current, list two specific design changes that would make an electromagnet stronger without changing the wire itself.
